title: One Van, Two Routes
story: Two couriers deliver along the same long street. Each route is a chain of stops, each pointing to the next, sorted by distance from the depot in metres.
One courier calls in sick, so one van must do both rounds in a single drive. The dispatcher needs one chain with every stop from both routes, still sorted by distance.
task: Write mergeRoutes(first, second). Both arguments are sorted linked lists (smallest distance first; null / None means no stops). Return the head of one sorted list that contains every node of both.
If both routes have a stop at the same distance, keep both stops. Reuse the existing nodes by relinking them rather than creating new ones.
constraints: -100,000 ≤ distance ≤ 100,000 (negative means west of the depot)
Each route is sorted in non-decreasing order.

examples.explanation: The merge takes 2 first because it is smaller than 3. It then takes 3, which is smaller than 5, then both 5s, then 9, which is smaller than 12, and finally the leftover 12.
The first courier had no stops, so the van follows the second route.

hints: Look only at the first stop of each route. Which must be the first stop of the merged route?
The smaller front stop goes first. Take it off its route, and you have the same question with one stop fewer.
Keep a tail pointer to the last merged stop so you can attach the next one in O(1). A dummy starting node means the first attachment is not a special case.

Create a dummy node and set tail = dummy. While both routes have stops, attach the smaller front node to tail.next, advance that route and advance tail. When one route runs out, attach the rest of the other in one step. Return dummy.next.
bruteForce: Copy every distance into an array, sort it, and build a new chain.
The sort costs O((n + m) log(n + m)), ignores that both routes were already sorted, and allocates a new chain. Merging walks each route once, O(n + m), and reuses the nodes.

walkthrough: The merged route starts with the smaller of the two front stops, and the same holds for what is left. So repeatedly compare the two fronts and move the smaller to the end of the result.
• The fronts are 2 and 3, so attach 2. The result is dummy → 2.
• The fronts are 5 and 3, so attach 3. The result is … → 2 → 3.
• The fronts are 5 and 5. They are equal, so take the first route's 5. The result is … → 3 → 5.
• The fronts are 9 and 5, so attach 5. The result is … → 5 → 5.
• The fronts are 9 and 12, so attach 9. The first route is now empty.
• Attach the rest of the second route, 12, in one step. Return dummy.next: 2 → 3 → 5 → 5 → 9 → 12.
The dummy node removes the "is the result still empty?" check. Without it, the first attachment needs special code, and that is where bugs hide.
solution.timeWhy: n and m are the two route lengths. Each step attaches one node, and every node is attached once.
solution.spaceWhy: The nodes are relinked, not copied. Only the dummy and a few pointers are extra.
solution.takeaway: To combine two sorted sequences, repeatedly take the smaller front item. Use a dummy head and a tail pointer whenever you build a linked list node by node. This merge step is the heart of merge sort.
